lead: Three distributions grow out of normal samples: chi-square, t and F. They describe sample variances and ratios of variances, and they let us use a sample mean when the population standard deviation is unknown. Chi-square is a sum of squared standard normals. t is a standard normal divided by a scaled chi-square. F is a ratio of two scaled chi-squares. They are used for means with unknown σ, variance checks, goodness of fit, variance ratios and ANOVA. This chapter defines each one, gives its mean and variance, and shows how the degrees of freedom fix its shape.
prereq: You need: the normal distribution (see Unit 3, Normal distribution) and the sampling distributions of the mean and variance from Chapter 5.2.

blocks.text: The chi-square distribution with ν degrees of freedom is written χ²(ν). Take ν independent standard normal variables Z₁, ..., Z_ν. Square each and add: χ²(ν) = Z₁² + ... + Z_ν². The degrees of freedom ν is the number of independent squared normals. The distribution is positive and right-skewed. Its mean is ν and its variance is 2ν. If ν = 10, the mean is 10 and the variance is 20. Chi-square appears when we study sample variance: for a normal population, (n−1)S²/σ² has χ²(n−1) df. Here n is sample size, S² is sample variance and σ² is population variance. It also measures how far observed counts are from expected counts in a goodness-of-fit test. Those tests are in Unit 6.

blocks.where: Z<sub>1</sub>, ..., Z<sub>ν</sub> are independent standard normal variables; ν is the degrees of freedom.

blocks.text: The t distribution is built from one standard normal and one chi-square. Let Z ~ N(0,1) and V ~ χ²(ν) be independent. Define T = Z / √(V/ν). Then T has a t distribution with ν degrees of freedom, written t(ν). The denominator √(V/ν) is random, so T has heavier tails than the standard normal. The t distribution is symmetric about 0, like the normal. As ν grows, t(ν) gets close to N(0,1); for small ν the tails are noticeably thick. Some syllabi call it Student's t distribution. We use t when the population standard deviation σ is unknown and the sample is small. For a sample of size n from a normal population, (X̄ − μ)/(S/√n) has t(n−1) df. Here X̄ is the sample mean, μ is the population mean, S is the sample standard deviation, and n is the sample size.

blocks.where: Z ~ N(0,1); V ~ χ²(ν); Z and V are independent; ν is the degrees of freedom.

blocks.text: The F distribution compares two chi-square variables. Let U ~ χ²(ν₁) and V ~ χ²(ν₂) be independent. Define F = (U/ν₁) / (V/ν₂). Then F has an F distribution with (ν₁, ν₂) degrees of freedom. ν₁ is the numerator df and ν₂ is the denominator df. F is positive and right-skewed, never symmetric. The order of df matters: F(5,10) is not F(10,5). If F ~ F(ν₁, ν₂), then 1/F ~ F(ν₂, ν₁). We use F for ratios of variances. For two independent normal samples, S₁²/S₂² scaled by the population variances has an F distribution. We also use F in analysis of variance (ANOVA) to compare several group means. Those test procedures are in Unit 6.

blocks.where: U ~ χ²(ν₁); V ~ χ²(ν₂); U and V are independent; ν₁ and ν₂ are the numerator and denominator degrees of freedom.

figure.caption: A standard normal and a chi-square with 10 df combine into t with 10 df; chi-squares with 5 and 10 df combine into F with 5 and 10 df.

spec.title: How t and F are built
spec.aria: A standard normal and a chi-square with 10 df form t with 10 df; chi-squares with 5 and 10 df form F with 5 and 10 df.

examples.question: Let Z ~ N(0,1) and V ~ χ²(10) be independent, and let T = Z/√(V/10). Find P(T ≤ 1.812). Also let U ~ χ²(5) and W ~ χ²(10) be independent, and let F = (U/5)/(W/10). Find the upper 5% point of F.
steps: By definition, T has a t distribution with ν = 10 df.
From the t table for 10 df, the 95th percentile is 1.812. So P(T ≤ 1.812) = 0.95.
F has an F distribution with numerator df ν₁ = 5 and denominator df ν₂ = 10.
From the F table for (5,10) df, P(F ≤ 3.33) = 0.95.
The upper 5% point leaves area 0.05 in the right tail, so it is F = 3.33.
examples.answer: P(T ≤ 1.812) = 0.95, and the upper 5% point of F(5,10) is 3.33.

traps: Using t when σ is known: if the population standard deviation is known, use the standard normal z, not t.
Mixing degrees of freedom: chi-square uses one ν, t uses one ν, F uses a pair (ν₁, ν₂).
Reversing numerator and denominator in F: F(5,10) and F(10,5) are different; 1/F swaps the two df.
Confusing mean and variance of chi-square: the mean is ν, the variance is 2ν, not ν².
Treating F as symmetric: F is positive and skewed, so upper and lower points are not negatives of each other.

quiz.q: State the definition of a chi-square variable with ν degrees of freedom.
quiz.a: χ²(ν) is the sum of squares of ν independent standard normal variables: χ²(ν) = Z₁² + ... + Z_ν².

quiz.q: Why does t(ν) have heavier tails than N(0,1)?
quiz.a: The denominator √(V/ν) is random and can be small. A small denominator makes the ratio large in absolute value, so extreme values are more likely than for a standard normal.

quiz.q: For χ²(10), find the mean and variance.
If U ~ χ²(5) and W ~ χ²(10) are independent, write a statistic with an F(5,10) distribution.
quiz.a: F = (U/5) / (W/10). The numerator df is 5 and the denominator df is 10.

quiz.q: If F ~ F(5,10) has upper 5% point 3.33, find the lower 5% point of F(10,5).
quiz.a: If F ~ F(5,10), then 1/F ~ F(10,5). The lower 5% point of F(10,5) is 1/3.33 = 0.30.

quiz.q: What is the role of degrees of freedom in these three distributions?
quiz.a: Degrees of freedom fix the shape. Chi-square and t use one df value ν; F uses two values (ν₁, ν₂). Larger df usually makes t closer to normal and makes chi-square less skewed.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, F distributions appear in quality control when comparing the variance of two production lines, and in A/B testing when comparing variation between groups. The t distribution is behind Welch's t-test, used when two groups have unequal variances. Chi-square appears in model fit checks and in count data. Search next for 'Welch t-test', 'Levene's test', 'F distribution ANOVA', and 'chi-square goodness of fit'.
